name: Clobetasol skin lightening

card.summary: Off-label use of a super-potent topical steroid, often found in unlabelled lightening creams, to even out or lighten skin tone.
card.note: Prescription-only in the US and not approved for lightening; reported harms include skin thinning, stretch marks and adrenal suppression.

quick.overview:
Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency corticosteroid used on the skin for conditions such as eczema, psoriasis and lichen sclerosus. Because corticosteroids reduce skin redness and can lighten skin, clobetasol appears in many skin-whitening creams, sometimes without being listed on the label.

People who use these products want a lighter or more even complexion, or fading of dark patches. Regulators in several regions, including the EU and the US, do not allow steroids in cosmetic products and the FDA has not approved clobetasol for lightening.
quick.how: In practice it appears as a cream or ointment sold either on prescription for dermatology conditions or as part of unregulated lightening products, often combined with hydroquinone or mercury. Users apply the products to the face or body over weeks or months.
quick.risks: Reported harms of long-term or widespread use include skin thinning and fragility, bruising, acne, stretch marks, high blood pressure, raised blood sugar and suppression of the body's own steroid production. Lightened skin is also more vulnerable to sun damage. People who are pregnant or have adrenal conditions are among those clinicians caution.

lead: Clobetasol propionate is a super-high-potency topical corticosteroid, in the highest of the seven classes of the US potency scale. It is prescribed for inflammatory skin diseases, and it is used off-label and in unregulated products to lighten skin tone [1].

In skin-lightening, steroids are among the most common ingredients, alongside mercury and hydroquinone. Wikipedia notes that clobetasol propionate is often used on specific patches of pigment and that steroids are frequently present in products without being listed [2]. Users describe the goal as a lighter, more uniform complexion.

Regulators and clinicians have documented a range of harms from prolonged steroid use on the skin. The EU does not allow corticosteroids in cosmetics, and the FDA has not approved clobetasol for lightening [1][2].

chain: Suppresses inflammation and pigment production in treated areas
angle.text: People use clobetasol-containing creams to lighten the skin or fade dark areas. It is used in the pigment-lightening category alongside hydroquinone and mercury products.

paras: Clobetasol propionate is prescribed for eczema, contact and seborrheic dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, alopecia areata and other conditions. It is a first-line treatment for skin graft-versus-host disease. It comes as a cream, foam, gel, solution, ointment or shampoo [1].

Corticosteroids are among the most common lightening agents in skin-whitening products and are used mainly to treat specific areas of pigmentation [2]. Wikipedia reports that illegally sold products, including some sold in beauty shops and online, may carry higher concentrations than prescription versions allow [1].

Skin lightening is practised widely. A summary on Wikipedia cites 2013 survey figures in which about 77 percent of Nigerian women, 52 percent of Senegalese women and 25 percent of Malian women reported using lightening products, and says that lightening formulations make up over half of skin-care sales in India [2].

Common effects of clobetasol include irritation, dryness, redness, pimples and visible small blood vessels. Serious effects include allergic reaction, cellulitis, adrenal suppression and Cushing's syndrome. Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding is unclear [1].

In the lightening context, reported harms include skin thinning, bruising, acne, stretch marks, high blood pressure, raised blood sugar and suppression of natural steroid production [1]. Long-term use over large areas increases absorption and has been linked with skin fragility, glaucoma, cataracts, oedema, osteoporosis, menstrual irregularities and growth suppression. Lightened skin is also reported to be more vulnerable to sun damage and infection [2].

Clobetasol propionate is prescription-only in the United States, and non-prescription sales are illegal there [1]. The EU does not allow corticosteroids in cosmetics because of side effects. Several countries prohibit lightening products with such ingredients, but Wikipedia reports that enforcement is often weak and banned compounds continue to appear in products sold [2].
No studies found on clobetasol as a skin lightener for healthy skin. Clinical research on the drug concerns inflammatory skin disease.

timeline.event: Surveys report high lightening-product use in several West African countries [2].
